cards.title: Pair Signature Sound With Logo to Boost Liking and Recall
cards.summary: Simultaneous congruent audio plus logo increases attention, pleasantness and long-term memory encoding versus either alone.
cards.use_when: Designing brand assets for a PDP, video ad, unboxing page or app: deciding whether to add a sonic signature, jingle or branded audio cue alongside your logo.
steps: Have one distinctive branded sound (jingle, sting, sonic logo) and one highly recognizable visual mark, then always present them together rather than separately.

In video and animated PDP media, time the sound to land exactly on the logo reveal so eyes and ears fire simultaneously; simultaneous pairing outperformed sound-only or image-only in Lindstrom's fMRI study.
Check congruence: the sound's mood must match the product category and imagery, since the positive results held when sound and vision were combined in a congruent way.

Test the pairing, not just the assets: measure whether the combined unit is liked and remembered, because a sound that is liked in isolation can still suppress feeling for the logo (the Nokia result).
For audio-only channels where a logo cannot appear, expect weaker liking and recall than the paired version and compensate with repetition or an additional visual cue elsewhere.
caveats: Findings come from a small lab fMRI study of four brands; three of four benefited from pairing, so treat it as a directional principle, not a guaranteed lift.
This is preference, emotional engagement and memory encoding data, not measured purchase lift.

cards.title: Audit Your Signature Sound for Negative Somatic Associations
cards.summary: A famous, ubiquitous brand sound can become a negative somatic marker that suppresses positive feeling for the visual brand.
cards.use_when: Reviewing an existing sonic identity, notification sound, hold music or app alert that has been in market for years and may now be associated with interruption.
steps: Recognize the Nokia pattern: the ring was among the most successfully branded tunes ever, yet when paired with Nokia imagery it produced across-the-board negative emotional response and dragged down preference for the phones themselves.
Investigate the context of exposure, not the melody. Negative associations came from where the sound was heard: a phone interrupting dinner, a movie, a yoga class, a call from the boss.
Watch for a tell in your own team: Lindstrom noticed an 'uncomfortable yikes feeling' when his own phone rang. Ask internal staff and customer-facing teams what feeling your sound triggers.

If the cue is a functional alert (order shipped, someone joined a call, doorbell, message), separate the functional alert from the branded marketing sound so the brand is not attached to interruption.
Test preference for your imagery with and without your signature sound. If the sound suppresses feeling for the logo, replace or retire it even if recall of the sound is high.
caveats: Source opinion: Lindstrom judged the Nokia tone was 'killing the brand' based on fMRI and rating data from his own study, not a sales regression.
Familiarity alone is not evidence of brand equity; high recall can coexist with negative affect.

cards.title: Multi-Sensory Congruence: Design Beyond Sight
cards.summary: Senses are intertwined in the brain, so the right pairing of smell, sound and touch with visuals makes a brand more engaging than visual-only design.
cards.use_when: Planning retail interiors, packaging, unboxing experience, brand film or event activation where you can add a non-visual cue on top of the visual identity.
steps: Pick the sense that carries the meaning you want, not just the loudest one. Lindstrom's vision of future retail links a lemon scent to sneakers, fresh orange to sporting goods, perfume to a hotel entrance.
Choose a congruent sensory note rather than a random pleasant one, since the benefit came from the right pairing of sensory inputs.

Build the cue into the physical product where it can carry association: GSK's Alli used vivid red, blue, yellow and green on white plus a uniquely shaped, portable 'shuttle' pill carrier with a gentle bubbled texture to evoke partnership and a journey together.
Repeat the cue across channels (packaging, store, site video, ad) so the sensory signal becomes a recognizable asset rather than a one-off stunt.
Track emotional engagement and recall in tests, not just stated liking, because stated preference diverges from measured response.
caveats: The Times Square smell-and-sound scenario is Lindstrom's prediction, not a documented result.
Scent and sound in ecommerce are largely limited to video, packaging and physical retail; browser-based scent is not a practical channel today.

cards.title: Test Congruent Cue Combinations, Not Single Cues
cards.summary: Sound-plus-image combinations were rated more favorably and left more impression than either element alone, but one brand's cue actively harmed the pairing.
cards.use_when: Setting up creative testing for ad or PDP assets where you plan to combine a logo, a jingle, a face, a color or a spokesperson.
steps: Structure the test as three arms minimum: cue A alone, cue B alone, and the combination, so you can see whether the pairing is additive, neutral or destructive.
Follow Lindstrom's run design: present the sound alone, then the image alone, then both simultaneously, and repeat the sequence to capture stable responses.
Include a neutral benchmark in each category (a generic ring tone, an unrelated image) because Nokia's ring made subjects prefer unrelated benchmark images over Nokia phones.

Interpret combination results in context, not in isolation: Microsoft's logo tested less positive than its sound, yet the joint presentation of logo and melody raised preference slightly, so combining can rescue a weaker element.
Decide the go/no-go on the combined asset's emotional engagement and long-term memory encoding if you have access to those measures, otherwise on recall and preference for the pair.
caveats: This is fMRI lab methodology; most ecommerce teams can only approximate it with survey-based recall and preference tests.
Results varied by brand, so a positive category-level pattern does not guarantee your pairing will be additive.

cards.title: Treat Stated Buy Intent as Unreliable for Launch Decisions
cards.summary: Questionnaire responses often do not match behavioral outcomes, so stated liking is a weak predictor of product or content success.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to launch a new product, SKU, bundle, landing page concept or ad campaign based on survey, focus group or concept-test feedback.
steps: Compare stated preference to a harder measure before committing budget. In Lindstrom's TV study, How Clean Is Your House? was a proven hit and The Swan a proven flop, yet the two scored neck and neck on viewers' stated likelihood to watch.
Collection note: the source text contains a corrupted character (a single letter) where one of the two scores would appear, so only the neck-and-neck conclusion is reliable.

Look for the divergence pattern: Quizmania was rated the show viewers would least likely watch, yet brain engagement landed between the flop and the hit, and it subsequently performed as the scans predicted in the U.K.

Use non-verbal or behavioral proxies available to an ecommerce team: actual click-through and add-to-cart for creative variants, or the eye-tracking-style attention data below, rather than stated intent alone.
Keep the benchmark logic: predict relative rank against known successes and known failures rather than an absolute pass/fail.
caveats: The brain-engagement method is not available to most merchants; the transferable lesson is skepticism toward stated intent, not the specific prediction method.
The 99 percent statistical certainty in the source refers to that study's confidence, not to any product launch prediction you make.

cards.title: Vampire Effect: Titillating Creative Steals Attention From the Brand
cards.summary: Sexual imagery draws gaze to itself and away from the brand name, reducing brand recall versus neutral creative.
cards.use_when: Reviewing acquisition creative, hero images, model photography or landing page visuals that are suggestive but may not be carrying your logo, product name or offer.
steps: Check what the image is actually competing with: MediaAnalyzer's eye-movement test found men spent inordinate time on breasts and largely bypassed brand name, logo and body text.

Compare recall numbers to decide whether the creative earns its place: brand recall was about 9.8 percent for men viewing sexual ads versus almost 20 percent for nonsexual ads, and about 10.85 percent versus 22.3 percent for women.

Reduce the problem by physically separating the provocative element from the information: keep logo, product name and price in a zone the eye must land on, or overlay the brand mark on or near the focal point.
Avoid stacking sexual creative on top of already sexual context, since viewers of Sex and the City had worse ad recall than viewers of a non-erotic sitcom, as the show's own content eclipsed the ads.
Measure brand recall, not just CTR, when testing this category of creative: a suggestive image may win clicks and still fail to lodge the brand.
caveats: The Eye-movement and recall studies used print ads and young adult samples, so figures are study-specific and not benchmarks for your store.
The conclusion attributed to Parker and Furnham is that sex 'does not sell anything other than itself', which is a strong generalization from their recall study.

cards.title: Choose Controversy Over Titillation When You Want Attention
cards.summary: Evidence points to controversy, not sexual content per se, being the more potent driver of attention and purchase influence.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a provocative campaign, limited drop or naming choice is worth the risk to brand perception.
steps: Separate the two levers in your planning: sexual content draws the eyes to itself (Vampire Effect), while controversy generates publicity and news coverage around the brand.

Consider the Calvin Klein pattern as a case study, not a playbook: the 1980 Brooke Shields campaign was reported to drive jeans sales up to roughly two million pairs a month, and by 1984 the business was worth nearly a billion dollars a year — but the source also notes sales have declined, the brand was sold to Phillips Van Heusen in 2002, and the same provocative ads these shoppers saw also drew boycotts, TV network refusals and a Justice Department investigation.

Weigh the reversibility of brand damage: pull ads generated fresh publicity (the pattern Lindstrom describes as a deliberate PR maneuver), but some brands suffered — the source says Dolce & Gabbana was hurt after a gang-rape-look ad was pulled under protest.
Decide the message in advance: an ad needs attention, the name in memory, and consistency. Nike's ad worked because the image pointed to product performance and brand, not to an unrelated sight gag.
Watch the boundary: controversy may drive short-term customers away while making the ad more memorable, so it is a trade, not a free win.
caveats: Controversy-driven growth claims are historical case observations, not controlled tests, and the source explicitly says the mechanism is unproven.
Boycotts and retailer refusals are real costs the source documents alongside the sales gains.

cards.title: Keep Sex and Attention-Getters Pointing at the Product
cards.summary: Attention-grabbing devices work when they direct attention to the product and misfire when they merely grab attention for themselves.
cards.use_when: Judging hero imagery, spokesperson choice, humour or shock value in an ad or PDP before committing spend.
steps: Ask what the viewer will look at and remember: if it is the joke, the model or the controversy rather than the product, the creative fails the Vampire Effect test.

Contrast pairs: the source presents a sexualized image of a dominatrix holding a vacuum cleaner, a suggestive toilet-paper image and a suggestive car ad as examples where the relevant connection is weak or absurd, while Nike's product-performance-toned campaign is presented as a case where the provocative image pointed straight at the product.

For ecommerce applications, adapt this to PDP video and social creative: the eye-catching element should be the product in use, or a demonstration of the claim, rather than a model or gag unrelated to it.

Check the exception: for fashion categories with a natural link between body and product (lingerie, fragrance, swimwear), the productive path is to keep the presentation on the product and its wearer, as the source argues Calvin Klein does.
If your only aim is clicks and the product link is weak, expect a short-lived spike and measure post-click quality (add-to-cart, return rate) rather than click volume.
caveats: The comparison set is Lindstrom's editorial selection of ads he saw, not a controlled experiment.
The source's own viewpoint is that most sexual advertising is 'harder to swallow', so treat the sex-versus-controversy distinction as his interpretation.

cards.title: Measure Before Believing: Human Responses Don't Match Stated Intent
cards.summary: People misreport why they say they can't wait to buy, because conscious and unconscious processes differ.
cards.use_when: Designing post-purchase surveys, NPS follow-ups, ad recall questions or any research meant to predict which product, offer or campaign will actually sell.
steps: Treat stated intent as a hypothesis to verify, not a finding: how we say we feel about a product cannot truly predict how we behave.
Design questions around past behaviour (what did you buy, when) — memory of actual past behaviour is more reliable than prediction of future behaviour.

Where possible, measure emotional response alongside rational response; in Lindstrom's TV study the brain data matched the show's real performance while the questionnaire did not match either show's real performance.
Keep a benchmark: include a product or campaign with known outcomes when testing new concepts so you can see whether the test can separate winners from losers at all.
Watch for the novelty effect: Lindstrom's team gave viewers the DVDs to watch and 'sleep on it' before scanning, to reduce the inflated response first-time viewing produces.
caveats: The source's own confidence is high, but the technique under test in his book is not considered settled science.
Some of the source's claims about fMRI methodology exceeding research capability are carried over from the research team, not independently proved.

cards.title: Run Quarterly NPS and Segment by Historical Value
cards.summary: NPS combines a simple recommendation question with open comments, and its business insight comes from linking responses to historical customer value and behaviour.
cards.use_when: Setting up recurring customer feedback for a store and deciding where to spend service, range, price and convenience effort.
steps: Ask the recommend question on a 0-10 scale repeatedly and consistently so you can track trend rather than one-off scores.

Do not collapse feedback into the score: read the comments for category-specific issues that word clouds hide, such as store cleanliness, staff attitude, price and range in the source's grocery example.

Link scores to historical transaction data: the source reports that for one business the most valuable customer segments were measurably more likely to be promoters, and that senior store managers whose locations scored well on service were more likely to exceed profit plans.
Use the feedback for budget decisions: the source describes how the NPS result redirected investment away from long-underfunded service areas toward store-level improvements.
Set an internal threshold for action and follow the score over time so you can tell whether a change moved the needle, rather than chasing a single survey cycle.
caveats: The source reports some of these findings as its own consulting analysis rather than as independently published results.
NPS is a public-domain measure with contested academic support, so treat it as one input alongside behavioural metrics.

cards.title: Use Recurring Research With Complaining and Non-Complaining Customers
cards.summary: Reichheld's approach pairs a simple recommendation survey with follow-up on the people who do not complain, then links answers to spending and retention.
cards.use_when: Building a customer research cadence for an ecommerce brand and deciding which responses should trigger a follow-up or win-back action.
steps: Ask a short, repeatable recommendation question with an open comment box.
Do not rely on complaints alone: the source's view is that unhappy customers who never complain are a hidden cost because the company believes they are satisfied.
Read comments at category level and watch for the gap between what leadership assumes and what the free text actually says, as the source describes for store cleanliness and staff attitude.

Use the closed-loop follow-up as the mechanism: Lindstrom describes a chief executive who called customers personally because 'that is how I learn', which is the spirit of following up rather than only scoring.
Tie results to spend behaviour where you can, since the source connects promoter likelihood to higher historical customer value and to store-level performance.
caveats: The 85 percent threshold for successful promoters and the segment-level comparisons in the source are reported as one consultancy's proprietary results, not independently verified.
A single survey cannot tell you why a customer behaves as they do; pair it with transaction data.

cards.title: Move Research Out of the Building to See Real Behaviour
cards.summary: Reichheld argues that companies spend too much time in internal meetings and not enough observing customers and front-line operations directly.
cards.use_when: Planning a product, pricing or merchandising decision and deciding how much effort to spend on direct customer contact versus internal deck reviews.
steps: Build direct observation into the calendar the way Lindstrom describes: personally working the front line and calling users is the version of 'getting out of the building' the source recommends.
Attend the touchpoints where your customers actually make decisions — search and product pages for a store, aisles and tills for physical locations — rather than reviewing reports about them.
Capture questions customers ask and objections they raise on the call, at the till, or in chats, and use them verbatim as inputs to copy and FAQ.
Push the observation habit down to senior managers so store-level or channel-level decisions are informed by their own observations, not just from reporting.
Reserve time for this every quarter; the source's criticism is that leaders drift toward internal meetings as the default.
caveats: This is executive practice guidance from the source, not a controlled study.
Direct observation is qualitative and should not replace measurement of conversion, retention and margin.

cards.title: Design Products That Fit the Way the Brain Works
cards.summary: Reichheld's closing argument is that product design should follow how the brain actually works rather than force people to think in a new way.
cards.use_when: Deciding on navigation, checkout flow, packaging format or subscription mechanics where users must learn a new pattern.
steps: Prefer the pattern that feels natural: the source's example is Amazon's Simple Storage Service, which won because it was simple, and TiVo, which lost because it left the user in no-man's-land between recording and watching television.

When you invent a new model, test whether users can predict what happens next: the failure mode in the TiVo example is that the software divided the mind and required the user to deal with a newly present and equal-demanding dual entity.
Apply this to subscription and replenishment design: keep control and expectations explicit so customers can see what will happen, when and how to change it.
Apply it to the site or app: use familiar, logical navigation and visible indicators (progress, stock, delivery estimates) so the user's mental model matches the interface.
Treat category-leading functionality as insufficient: the source argues that superior products can still fail on usability and that better understanding of the brain improves both design and service.
caveats: TiVo and Amazon are Lindstrom's chosen examples of design principles, not tested experiments in the book.
Underestimating the next big idea is a risk the source also acknowledges; simplicity should not be read as 'never innovate'.
